To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

sequential catheter-based interventions for coronary artery disease (or other vascular beds), renovascular disease (or other) and peripheral artery disease in a single stage are feasible, safe and effective.
in our study population sequential catheter-based interventions were performed in different vascular beds with high success rates.
sequential catheter-based interventions of two different vascular bed can be performed in a safe and effective manner in patients with multimorbidity.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether it is possible to perform two different catheter-based interventions on two different vascular beds (e.g. coronary artery disease (cad) and renovascular hypertension (rvh), cad and peripheral artery disease) in a single stage, thus avoiding a second intervention.
the question of how the combination of coronary artery disease (CABG) and peripheral artery disease can be successfully treated.
the development of a novel, non-invasive, non-ionizing and non-contact optical method for the detection of blood flow in the coronary arteries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a single stage approach may be a safe and feasible alternative to a staged procedure.
single-stage catheter-based interventions of two different vascular bed are safe and effective.
a single-stage approach in patients with vascular multi-morbidity is feasible, safe and effective, however, the risk of access site complications may be increased.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the combination of two different catheter-based interventions can be performed in a one stage approach with a high success rate, however, compared with the literature, possibly at a higher risk for complications at the vascular access sites.
the treatment of vascular multimorbidity in a single stage is feasible and may be beneficial for selected patients.
a single-stage approach to vascular disease may be a feasible strategy in patients with vascular disease, but that further research is needed to assess its efficacy and cost effectiveness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the single stage approach is feasible and can be performed safely.
the combination of different vascular interventions in a single stage is feasible and safe.
the single stage approach is feasible in patients with clinically significant vascular multimorbidity.
